Before you start

Students learn why people freeze, and pick one of four moves (distract, delegate, direct, delay) that's safe for them, with a line ready ahead of time. Bring index cards, use only the moments on the slides, and take anything real to a counselor or dean that day.

Every student in the room

Speaking up costs some students more than others, so present all four moves as equal, and keep bodies out of the locker room discussion.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open plainly: “You all know the word upstander. Today is about why it’s so hard in the moment, and what makes the difference.” Say up front that nobody will share real incidents or real names, and that everything today is optional to say out loud.

Slide 2 · Notes

Collect the cards, shuffle them, and tally out loud. Most circles land mostly on yes. That’s the point: freezing is common, and it usually means you got stuck somewhere. If anyone wrote more than yes or no, read it privately afterward, and follow up with a counselor that day if it points to something ongoing.

Slide 3 · Notes

Every gate is a place to drop out and a place to get through. Pair-share for two minutes: “Which gate do you get stuck at most?” Expect gate 2 (“it’s just a joke”), gate 3 (“someone else will”) and gate 4 (“I don’t know what to say”). Online every gate gets harder: easy not to notice, easy to call it a joke, easy to assume someone else will report it.

Slide 4 · Notes

This is a 1968 study with college students. Take a few guesses for each. The next slide shows the numbers.

Slide 5 · Notes

More people listening, less help. Not because they were bad people: each one assumed someone else was already on it. That’s gate 3.

Slide 6 · Notes

These were playground studies with younger kids. Take guesses. The next slide shows the number, and what happened when someone did step in.

Slide 7 · Notes

Those were younger kids, and high school is more complicated. But the people watching hold a lot of power. More good news is on the next slide.

Slide 8 · Notes

Security-camera footage from three countries. The bystander effect is real in a lab, but in real life someone usually steps in, and it gets weaker when the danger is clear and when bystanders know each other.

Slide 9 · Notes

Take a few answers from the circle. The next slide shows what usually comes up.

Slide 10 · Notes

Point out the middle-school study: it worked best when the group included students others paid attention to. Anyone in this room can be that student for someone.

Slide 11 · Notes

You don’t need a speech. Distract interrupts without confronting anyone. Delegate is using your resources, and it counts as stepping in. Direct is one sentence, then move on, and only if it feels safe. Delay is never too late, and people remember who did it. Including someone who keeps ending up on the edge counts too. What usually backfires: getting physical (get an adult), and forwarding something to show it’s wrong (sharing spreads it).

Slide 12 · Notes

Lead with what students bring: knowing what it’s like, a second language, a family or faith that taught them to show up. Then name that speaking up costs some students more than others, so the four moves are equal. Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 13 · Notes

Talk through it as a circle, or pairs then a quick share. Keep the talk on the move, not on the body or the comment. More than one answer works; the best one is the one you’d actually do. The next slide shows one good move.

Slide 14 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 15 · Notes

Pairs decide. “It’s not my business” is gate 3. Keep the talk on Ana and on what friends can do together. The next slide shows one good move.

Slide 16 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 17 · Notes

Pairs decide. A reaction is still joining in. Some students in your circle may have been mocked for an accent: keep the focus on what a bystander can do, and never ask anyone to explain what it feels like. The next slide shows one good move.

Slide 18 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 19 · Notes

Gate 4 is easier when the line is ready before you need it. If students are stuck, offer examples out loud: “Not funny.” “I’m not sending that around.” “Would you say that if they were standing here?” “You okay? That was messed up.” Nobody shares unless they want to.

Slide 20 · Notes

Turn and talk, partners by seat. Then ask: “Where else in your life does this show up?” Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 21 · Notes

Share the student page link. Close with: “Everyone has frozen. A late check-in still counts.” The same person getting targeted over and over, or worrying you’ll be next, is a good reason to talk to a counselor.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can name the five gates between seeing something and doing something, explain why freezing is common, and pick one of four moves (distract, delegate, direct, delay) that is safe for them, with a line ready before they need it. Nobody shares a real incident or a real name.

Materials

  • Index cards: one per student, for the anonymous yes/no and the private line
  • A board or sheet of paper for the tally
  • The student page link (last slide) to share after advisory

Flow

  1. 3 minHave you ever frozen? (anonymous cards)
  2. 4 minFive gates (pair-share: where do you get stuck?)
  3. 3 minSomeone usually steps in, and it works
  4. 2 minFour ways to step in
  5. 5 minThree moments (scenario talk)
  6. 2 minYour line (private card)
  7. 1 minOne move, and the student page link

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Anonymous cards and the tally (3), the five gates with a quick pair-share (3), one scenario with the four moves (3), close and the link (1).

Before you teach
No real incidents, no real names.

Use only the moments on the slides. Don't ask students to describe something they saw or did. Someone in your circle may be the target of something right now, and someone may have been part of it.

If a real situation comes up, take it out of the circle.

If a student names something ongoing, thank them, say you want to help with it privately, and move on. Follow up that day with a counselor or dean.

Know what needs an adult right away.

Someone being physically hurt or threatened, private or sexual images being shared (real or AI-made), or someone saying they want to hurt themselves or others. Don't ask about these in advisory. Any disclosure goes to a counselor the same day.

Telling an adult will feel like snitching to some students.

Name that worry out loud. Delegating means bringing in someone with more power, and it counts as stepping in. Say plainly what happens at Beaver when a student reports something, so it feels less like a leap.

Leave room for past silence.

Most students have frozen at least once, and some have laughed along. Keep shame out of it. A late check-in still counts, and what matters is the next time.

Don't rank the moves.

Direct can look like the brave one. It isn't always safe, and getting physical is never the move. Every one of the four counts, and so does including someone who keeps ending up on the edge.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Speaking up costs some students more.

A comment that costs one student nothing might cost another more, because of race, gender, size, being new, or how people already treat them. Say this out loud, and let students choose the move that is safe for them.

The accent scenario may be close to home.

Some students in your circle speak another language at home or have been mocked for an accent. Keep the focus on what a bystander can do. Never ask a student to explain what it feels like or to speak for a group.

Gender scripts show up in the locker room and the party.

Boys can check on a teammate and say "not funny" without it being soft. In the party scenario, keep the talk on the person who looks uncomfortable and on what friends can do together.

Targeting about identity is a same-day conversation.

If a student is being harassed about their sexuality, gender identity, race, or religion, or someone is outing them, that goes to a counselor that day. The Trevor Project (call 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678) is there for LGBTQ+ young people any time.

Speaking up isn't the only way to be brave.

Students with social anxiety, a stutter, or who process slowly in the moment may freeze longer or find Direct hard. Delay, Delegate and Distract count just as much. Don't treat speaking out loud as the measure of a good person.

Keep bodies out of the locker room discussion.

The first scenario is about a comment on someone's body. Talk about the move, not the body or the comment. Students of every size are in the circle.

What the research says

Before a bystander helps, they have to get through five steps: notice, decide it's a problem, feel it's theirs to act on, know what to do, and act. Getting stuck at any step looks like freezing.

Latané and Darley, The Unresponsive Bystander, 1970

Students who heard someone over an intercom seem to have a seizure went for help before the call cut off 85% of the time when they thought they were alone, and 31% of the time when they thought four others could hear.

Darley and Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1968

A review of studies with more than 7,700 people confirmed the bystander effect, and found it gets weaker when a situation is clearly dangerous and when bystanders know each other.

Fischer et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2011

In security-camera footage of 219 real public fights in the UK, the Netherlands and South Africa, at least one bystander did something to help in 9 of 10. More people around made help more likely.

Philpot et al., American Psychologist, 2020

On school playgrounds, peers were present for 88% of bullying episodes but stepped in during only 19%. When they did, the bullying stopped most of the time (57%). These were younger children.

Hawkins, Pepler and Craig, Social Development, 2001

In 56 New Jersey middle schools with more than 24,000 students, small groups of students who took a public stand against conflict cut disciplinary reports of conflict by 25% in a year. The effect was strongest when the group included students others paid attention to.

Paluck, Shepherd and Aronow, PNAS, 2016
